sections.title: Participants in the Public Policy Process
The Making of a Public Policy

slides.title: Policies All Around You
slides.kicker: Your whole morning runs on public policies
bullets: Roads we travel on, traffic signals that help us cross safely, and clean drinking water at home all come from public policies.
Electricity that lights our classrooms, public parks where we play, and neighbourhood waste collection are public services too.
Public policies work quietly in the background, making our daily lives safer, healthier, and more convenient.
slides.note: Spot one public service on your way to school.

slides.title: The Plastic-Free Campus
slides.kicker: Ek school story that shows what policy means
bullets: Students brought single-use plastic bottles and wrappers every day, so waste piled up and the campus slowly degraded the environment.
The principal discussed the issue with teachers, students, and parents, and together they introduced a Plastic-Free Campus Policy.
Reusable bottles encouraged, plastic bags discouraged, segregation dustbins placed, monthly awareness programmes, teachers monitored.
These decisions form a policy because they give a planned course of action to solve a problem and reach a sustainable goal.
slides.note: One school problem, one planned course of action.

slides.title: What Public Policy Means
slides.kicker: The government's planned answer to society's problems
bullets: Public policy is a course of action adopted by the government to solve public problems and promote the welfare of society.
It decides what should be done, why, who will do it, how it will be implemented, and how success will be measured.
The policy is monitored and evaluated through a feedback loop, and necessary changes are made to it if required.
slides.note: Policy is a loop, not a full stop.

slides.title: What Makes It Public
slides.kicker: Made by the public, for the public, with public money
bullets: The word public refers to all the people living in a society or community.
A policy becomes public when it is made for public benefit, implemented by public institutions, and often financed through taxes.
Public policies address issues that concern society as a whole, like education, healthcare, transportation, sanitation, and public safety.
Public policy responds to the needs and aspirations of the people, so people play an important role in it.

slides.title: Not Just the Government
slides.kicker: Who really decides what gets built and fixed?
bullets: Who decides if new schools are built, roads are repaired, or taxes are changed? Not the government alone.
It takes the combined efforts of many individuals, organisations, officials, and even ordinary citizens.
Together they identify issues, provide solutions, and put them into action.
slides.note: Democracy is a team game, not a solo match.

slides.title: Citizens and Representatives
slides.kicker: From a zebra crossing request to an Assembly question
bullets: Citizens identify problems, vote, participate, give suggestions, and give feedback, like residents seeking a zebra crossing.
Elected representatives, MPs, MLAs, and local representatives, represent people, raise public issues, make laws, and approve budgets.
An MLA raising the issue of drinking water shortage in the Assembly shows people's voices reaching the House.
slides.note: One request can start real change.

slides.title: Officials, Experts and Media
slides.kicker: The hands that prepare, deliver, and watch closely
bullets: Officials, departments, and ministries of Central, State, and Local governments prepare and implement policies and programmes.
They coordinate departments, deliver public services, and monitor progress, like a district collector coordinating a scheme.
Civil society organisations, NGOs, experts, researchers, and the media study problems, suggest solutions, and create awareness.
An NGO ran a water-conservation campaign while the media highlighted pollution concerns.

slides.title: Business and the World
slides.kicker: Partners bring technology, resources, and global experience
bullets: The private sector facilitates technical know-how, innovation, resources, and expertise, often working with the government.
A company installing solar panels in government schools through a public-private partnership shows this teamwork.
International organisations bring international experience, technical know-how, and financial support.
The World Health Organization assists countries in controlling infectious diseases.
slides.note: PPP means public and private working together.

slides.title: A Cycle, Not One Decision
slides.kicker: Good policy grows through a systematic cycle
bullets: A public policy is developed through a systematic process rather than a single decision.
It begins when citizens, officials, researchers, or civil society realise a new need, an existing problem, or a facility to improve.
The cycle runs through problem identification, consultation, policy formulation, implementation, monitoring, evaluation, and improvement.
This continuous cycle helps the government respond effectively to the changing needs of society.
slides.note: A policy is never really finished.

slides.title: From Study to Draft
slides.kicker: Listen first, consult widely, then write the draft
bullets: The government studies the issue, collects information, and consults experts, stakeholders, and the public.
These discussions reveal different viewpoints and possible solutions.
Based on them, the authorities prepare, review, and approve a draft policy.
Once approved, the policy becomes programmes and schemes, giving ministries, departments, and local bodies a clear framework to act.

slides.title: Early Stages of the Cycle
slides.kicker: From a felt need to a signed law
bullets: Policy desirability asks what needs and problems are to be addressed.
Prioritising policy decides which issues need to be addressed on a priority basis.
Policy formulation means consultation with stakeholders, drafting the policy, and assessing financial feasibility.
Policy adoption frames the legislation, the laws governing the policy, and the regulations, the rules and guidelines.
slides.note: Pehle samjho, phir priority, phir kanoon.

slides.title: Action and Follow-Through
slides.kicker: A policy on paper helps nobody
bullets: Policy implementation puts the policy into action through officials, local bodies, civil societies, private organisations, and citizens.
Policy monitoring measures the policy's progress, ensures accountability, and identifies shortcomings.
Policy evaluation assesses the results and impact of the policy and generates feedback.
Feedback from citizens and stakeholders is used to improve the policy over time.
slides.note: After launch, the real exam begins.

slides.title: NEP 2020, a Real Journey
slides.kicker: A policy written with the whole country's voice
bullets: The National Education Policy 2020 shows how policy is built through consultation, expert advice, and public participation.
India's previous National Policy on Education was introduced in 1986.
Over time, society changed rapidly, so the country crafted a new education policy for new times.

slides.title: Coordination Makes It Work
slides.kicker: Many departments, one mission, zero confusion
bullets: Policy coordination among different government departments, institutions, and stakeholders is essential for addressing public problems.
It is equally essential for responding to emergencies and delivering public services efficiently.
When departments and institutions move together, public services reach people smoothly and on time.

slides.title: Citizens Power Democracy
slides.kicker: Voting is only the beginning of your part
bullets: Active citizen participation means voting, giving feedback, obeying laws, community involvement, and holding authorities accountable.
Such participation strengthens democracy and promotes good governance.
Coordination is a two-way street: institutions must align, and citizens must engage.
slides.note: Democracy grows with every active citizen.

slides.title: Why Coordination Matters
slides.kicker: When one department stalls, the mission stalls
bullets: Most public problems touch many departments at once, so no single office can solve them alone.
That is why coordination among departments, institutions, and stakeholders is essential for public problems and emergencies alike.
Efficient delivery of public services is the everyday payoff of good coordination.
slides.note: Think relay race, not solo sprint.

slides.title: Argue and Reflect
slides.kicker: Time to think like a policymaker
bullets: Is good governance the responsibility of the government alone? Question one asks you to decide and defend your view.
Question two asks whether students can contribute, through five ways of becoming more responsible and active citizens.
Question four wants one-line answers on governance, its difference from government, public policy, and four principles of good governance.
Question five asks you to compare government with governance, and policy with public policy, in table form.

slides.title: Your Policy Chart Project
slides.kicker: Pick one mission and map its whole journey
bullets: Choose one public policy: Right to Education, Swachh Bharat Mission, PM POSHAN, Ayushman Bharat, Digital India, or Jal Jeevan Mission.
Prepare a chart showing the problem it addresses and the major stakeholders involved.
Also show how different actors coordinate and the role of citizens in its success.
Then present your findings to the class.
slides.note: One chart, one policy's full story.

slides.title: Prioritise and Diagnose
slides.kicker: Three picks only, policymaker, choose wisely
bullets: As advisor to the district administration you must choose three priority areas from your six proposals.
The six: drinking water in schools, sanitation and public toilets, tricycles for orthopaedically challenged students, park swings.
Plus stray dog vaccination to prevent rabies, and iron and folic acid tablets for female students in schools.
The tree case: funds flowed for one lakh trees, but only a few saplings survived, since none were watered or protected.

flashcards.back: Roads and traffic signals, clean drinking water, classroom electricity, public parks, and neighbourhood waste collection.

flashcards.front: What three things make a policy public?
flashcards.back: It is made for public benefit, implemented by public institutions, and often financed with public money collected through taxes.

flashcards.front: Why did the school's plastic decisions count as a policy?
flashcards.back: They formed a planned course of action to solve a problem and achieve a sustainable goal.

flashcards.front: Who are the key participants in the public policy process?
flashcards.back: Citizens, elected representatives, government officials and departments, NGOs, experts, media, the private sector, and international organisations.

flashcards.front: What roles do citizens play in policy-making?
flashcards.back: They identify problems, vote, participate, give suggestions, and provide feedback, like requesting a zebra crossing near a school.

flashcards.front: What do elected representatives do in the policy process?
flashcards.back: They represent people, raise public issues, participate in law-making, and approve budgets.

flashcards.front: Give the book's example of a public-private partnership.
flashcards.back: A company installed solar panels in government schools through a public-private partnership.

flashcards.front: How does the World Health Organization help countries?
flashcards.back: It brings international experience, technical know-how, and financial support, assisting countries in controlling infectious diseases.

flashcards.back: The stage that asks what needs and problems of the people are to be addressed.

flashcards.front: What happens during policy formulation?
flashcards.back: Consultation with various stakeholders, drafting the policy, and assessing financial feasibility.

flashcards.front: What happens during policy adoption?
flashcards.back: Framing the legislation, the laws governing the policy, and the regulations, the rules and guidelines.

flashcards.back: Monitoring measures progress, ensures accountability, and spots shortcomings; evaluation assesses results, impact, and generates feedback.

flashcards.back: India's previous National Policy on Education was introduced in 1986.

flashcards.front: Why is policy coordination essential?

flashcards.front: What does active citizen participation strengthen?

quiz.q: Which of these is a public service made possible through public policies?
options: A shopping mall's weekend discount sale
Traffic signals that help us cross safely
A video game's paid new skin
quiz.why: The book lists traffic signals, roads, drinking water, parks, and waste collection as services from public policies.

quiz.q: In the school story, what problem did the Plastic-Free Campus Policy tackle?
options: Waste from single-use plastic bottles and wrappers
quiz.why: Students brought single-use plastic daily, creating waste and dirtying the campus.

quiz.q: A policy becomes a public policy when it is...
options: printed as a thick government book
for public benefit, run by public institutions, financed by taxes
decided by one officer without discussion
quiz.why: Public benefit, public institutions, and public money through taxes make a policy public.

quiz.q: Which question is NOT part of what a public policy decides, per the book?
options: Which private company earns the most profit
quiz.why: The book lists what, why, who, how, and how to measure success, never private profit.

quiz.q: Residents requested a zebra crossing near a school. Which stakeholder group were they acting as?
quiz.why: Citizens identify problems and give feedback, like the zebra crossing request.

quiz.q: Which organisation does the book name for helping countries control infectious diseases?
quiz.why: The World Health Organization assists countries in controlling infectious diseases.

quiz.q: An MLA raises a drinking water shortage in the Assembly. Which stakeholder role does this show?
options: Representing people and raising public issues
quiz.why: Elected representatives raise public issues, participate in law-making, and approve budgets.

quiz.q: Who prepares and implements policies, coordinates departments, and monitors progress?
quiz.why: This is the book's description of officials, departments, and ministries across all levels.

quiz.q: A company installs solar panels in government schools. The book uses this to illustrate...
options: The private sector partnering with government
quiz.why: It is the book's public-private partnership example of private-sector technical know-how.

quiz.q: Putting the policy into action is called...
quiz.why: Implementation puts the policy into action through officials, local bodies, civil societies, and citizens.

quiz.q: Framing the legislation and regulations happens at which stage?
quiz.why: The policy cycle frames laws and rules during policy adoption.

quiz.q: Which stage combines stakeholder consultation, drafting, and checking financial feasibility?
quiz.why: Policy formulation is consultation, drafting, and assessing financial feasibility.

quiz.q: Which stage decides which issues must be addressed on a priority basis?
quiz.why: Prioritising policy decides which issues need attention first.

quiz.q: Progress is measured, accountability ensured, shortcomings identified. Which stage is this, and what follows?
quiz.why: Monitoring measures progress and finds shortcomings; evaluation then assesses impact and feedback improves the policy.

quiz.q: Which of these is part of active citizen participation?
quiz.why: The book lists voting, feedback, obeying laws, community involvement, and holding authorities accountable.

quiz.q: Policy coordination among departments is essential for all of these EXCEPT...
quiz.why: The book links coordination to public problems, emergencies, and efficient public services.

quiz.q: Which chain best matches the book's argument in this section?
options: Coordination handles problems and emergencies, while citizen participation strengthens democracy
Coordination replaces the need for elections
Citizens should only pay taxes and stay uninvolved
Coordination matters only for private companies
quiz.why: Coordination serves public problems and emergencies; active participation strengthens democracy and good governance.

quiz.q: Assessing the impact of a policy belongs to which policy cycle stage?
quiz.why: Question seven's matching places impact assessment at policy evaluation.

quiz.q: In the tree case, funds flowed but few saplings survived. Which stages clearly failed?
quiz.why: Saplings were not watered or protected, so action on the ground and progress tracking failed.

quiz.q: You may keep only three of the six district proposals. The strongest welfare-first set is...
options: Park swings and open-air gym, stray dog vaccination, tricycles
School drinking water, sanitation and public toilets, iron and folic acid tablets
Stray dog vaccination, park swings, drinking water
quiz.why: Water, sanitation, and nutrition are daily basic needs of students, the welfare core of public policy.

quiz.q: Which two comparisons does question five ask you to present in table form?
options: Government vs governance, and policy vs public policy
quiz.why: Question five lists exactly those two comparisons.

examples.title: The Plastic-Free Campus Policy Cycle
examples.problem: A school notices that many students bring single-use plastic bottles and wrappers in their lunchboxes and schoolbags every day. A large amount of waste is generated, the campus becomes dirty, and the environment degrades in the long run. Show how the school's response becomes a complete policy cycle.
steps: Problem identification: daily single-use plastic waste is dirtying the campus and degrading the environment in the long run.
Consultation: the principal discusses the issue with teachers, students, and parents to gather different viewpoints.
Formulation and adoption: together they introduce the Plastic-Free Campus Policy, a planned course of action for a sustainable goal.
Implementation: reusable water bottles are encouraged, plastic bags are discouraged, and dustbins for waste segregation are placed around the campus.
Monitoring and evaluation: monthly awareness programmes are organised and teachers are assigned to monitor the campaign, so feedback can adjust the rules.
examples.answer: The school's decisions form a policy because they provide a planned course of action to solve a problem and achieve a sustainable goal.

examples.title: Mapping Stakeholders for a Zebra Crossing
examples.problem: Residents near a school want a zebra crossing on a busy road. Using the book's stakeholder table, show who does what to move the request from complaint to crossing.
steps: Citizens identify the problem and give feedback: residents request a zebra crossing near the school.
Elected representatives raise the public issue and support law-making and budgets, just as an MLA raised a drinking water shortage in the Assembly.
Government officials and departments prepare and implement the plan, the way a district collector coordinates the implementation of a government scheme in the district.
Civil society, experts, and the media create awareness and monitor, as an NGO's water-conservation campaign and media coverage of pollution concerns show.
The combined efforts of all participants identify the issue, provide the solution, and put it into action.
examples.answer: Policy is a team effort: citizens identify, representatives raise, officials implement, and civil society and media create awareness and monitor.

examples.title: Sorting Actions into the Policy Cycle
examples.problem: Match each policy action to its correct stage: assessing the impact of the policy, putting the policy into action, framing the legislation, multi-dimensional consultation with stakeholders, and addressing a new need of the people.
steps: Addressing a new need of the people is policy desirability, the stage that asks what needs and problems are to be addressed.
Multi-dimensional consultation with stakeholders, along with drafting and assessing financial feasibility, is policy formulation.
Framing the legislation and the regulations is policy adoption.
Putting the policy into action through officials, local bodies, civil societies, private organisations, and citizens is policy implementation.
Assessing the results and impact of the policy, which generates feedback, is policy evaluation.
examples.answer: Desirability, formulation, adoption, implementation, evaluation: five actions matched to five stages of the policy cycle.

examples.title: Diagnosing the Tree Plantation Programme
examples.problem: A government programme aims to plant one lakh trees in a city. Funds are allocated, but only a few saplings survive because they are not watered or protected. Identify which policy stages failed and how the programme could improve.
steps: Problem identification and funding worked: the city recognised a need and allocated funds for one lakh trees.
Implementation failed on the ground: saplings were not watered or protected after planting.
Monitoring failed too: nobody measured progress or identified the shortcoming of dying saplings in time.
Evaluation with citizen feedback would have exposed the poor survival rate and its causes.
Improvement for the next cycle: assign watering and protection duties, track sapling survival regularly, and use feedback to strengthen the programme.
examples.answer: Implementation and monitoring broke down; watering, protection, regular tracking, and feedback would make the next policy cycle succeed.
